15.0.0.en: "Drew near unto him for to hear him": they felt their need to hear His teachings, in which there is hope for sinners of repentance and life with God.

15.0.1.en: "This man": they meant to belittle Christ because He mingled with sinners.

15.0.2.en: "Eateth with them": He went further in associating with sinners, and Christ meant by this to find a greater opportunity to teach them and draw them to repentance.

15.0.3.en: The Law provided for avoiding the wicked so that we do not share in their evils, but the Pharisees and scribes were excessive in carrying out the Law because of their pride, so they despised sinners and also those who collect taxes (the tax collectors), because tax collecting was linked with harshness, exploitation and love of money. They overlooked the importance of caring for sinners and drawing them to repentance; rather, in their excess they accused Christ of evil because He mingled with them, although Christ was concerned with calling sinners to repentance. Therefore He welcomed them and was able to draw some of them not only to repentance but to service, like St. Matthew the Evangelist, who was a tax collector.

15.1.0.en: Because love for sinners and compassion for them were far from the hearts of the Pharisees, Christ presented it to them in a parable, that perhaps they might understand and their hearts be softened.

15.2.0.en: "Until he find it": the shepherd does not rest but keeps looking for his lost sheep until he finds it and it returns to the fold.

15.2.1.en: The parable He gave is of a man who has a hundred sheep feeding in the wilderness where there is greenery, and when he returned with them to their fold he found one of them missing, so he left the ninety and nine and went out looking for the lost sheep. The shepherd signifies Christ, who left His ninety and nine sheep, who are the angels, in the fold, which is heaven, and became incarnate to seek Adam and his sons, "the lost sheep."

15.2.2.en: Here He makes clear the importance of the one soul that the shepherd or servant seeks, who is not preoccupied with the ninety and nine who are faithful to the Church, because the ninety and nine are secure in their holding fast to God, while the person who has strayed needs more than all.

15.3.0.en: When the shepherd found the lost sheep he did not rebuke it, since he found it worn out from its straying and long walking, so he carried it on his shoulders with love and pride because it has great value in his heart, and he returned with it to the fold and called those who love him to rejoice with him over the lost sheep that returned to live with its brothers.

15.3.1.en: Just as Christ carried our sins on His shoulders when He was hung on the cross, then went down to Hades and brought up Adam and his sons, and the angels rejoiced in Paradise at man's return to his first place with them, so the whole Church rejoices at the sinner's return, and the servant cares for him more than for all, to heal his wounds with which he was wounded in the period of his straying, as the members of the Church take care to welcome him.

15.4.0.en: Heaven rejoices at the sinner's return because he was lost, while the ninety and nine are at ease in their relationship with God. In addition, when the sinner returns he is eager to make up for what he missed, so he rushes along the spiritual way and may surpass those who did not stray like him, because of the slackness of some of them.

15.4.1.en: There is another interpretation, that the ninety and nine just persons are righteous in their own eyes, so they feel they do not need repentance, and therefore the heavenly ones rejoice over this one sinner because he is repentant. Do not be occupied with the many and forget the distant person, but give him of your love even if you grow very tired for his sake, and if he refuses your love do not forget him in your prayer, and repeat the attempt to seek him as much as you can bear.

15.5.s.en: (2) The parable of the lost coin

15.5.0.en: Among His hearers were some shepherds, so He gave them the parable of the lost sheep, and He also found some women, so He gave the parable of the lost coin, to confirm the importance of the one soul in His sight and to call us to have compassion on sinners and those who are far.

15.5.1.en: A Jewish woman was given ten drachmas at her marriage, so they had more value for her than their ordinary value. If one of them was lost, she would look for it with concern and light her lamp to reveal some of the dark corners in her house, and not rest until she found it.

15.5.4.en: The fall of man caused Christ to become incarnate, to shine by His life as a lamp for humanity and reveal to it the way of salvation by examining the aspects of its life (sweeping the house) through His holy teachings, and then to rescue it by His redemption on the cross and bring it back to Paradise.

15.5.5.en: How great is the duty of the servants in seeking the distant person in all the wanderings of life, and the duty of the fathers of confession in alerting souls to know their sins, so that they receive forgiveness and life in Christ.

15.6.0.en: The woman calls her friends to rejoice with her over the lost coin that she found, as the Church calls the triumphant part of it, that is, the heavenly ones, to rejoice at the return of sinners.

15.6.1.en: The Church's love and sense of responsibility appear in her saying that she "lost" it, although it is the person who strayed and refused life in the Church; but her love as a mother seeks after him out of her responsibility for his being lost, until she finds him. Do not be content with rebuking sinners, but first look at what love you have given them and what you can give now, for you are responsible for the return of these sinners, and with God's help you can bring them back to the Church's embrace.

15.7.s.en: (3) The parable of the prodigal son

15.7.0.en: This parable is one of the most famous parables of Christ, showing God's love for sinners and His abundant gifts to them if they repent.

15.7.1.en: The younger son signifies the Gentiles, or the sinners and tax collectors among the Jews.

15.7.2.en: The elder son signifies the Jews, or the scribes and Pharisees, or the proud in general, especially those connected with the spiritual life.

15.7.4.en: In rebellion, contrary to custom, the son asked his father for his share of the inheritance and did not wait until his death. This means his neglect of enjoying his father's house, that is, the Church, and his lack of understanding of her care. The father, out of tenderness, agreed and gave him his share of the inheritance, and he took it and journeyed into a far country, which is selfishness.

15.7.5.en: Since this son loved himself more than he loved his father, he became estranged from the divine love through his falling into the self, and supposed that his happiness was in it and in satisfying its material desires.

15.7.6.en: "Wasted his substance": that is, all his energies, gifts and senses on the passing things of the world, until he squandered them wastefully without awareness.

15.7.7.en: The devil deceives you that freedom is satisfying your material desires, and makes you forget that you lose your sonship to God and His care for you. So obey the commandment to keep your sonship in the Church.

15.8.0.en: The prodigal son was immersed in his desires and spent all the money he had until it ran out, and he found no food to sustain him. He was surprised by a famine throughout the country to which he had gone, and so he found no one to give him anything to eat, and he was forced to look for work to live from, and found only lowly work, which was feeding swine, which are marked by filthiness. His wage was small and did not suffice for his sustenance, so he longed to eat of the food of the animals he was feeding, which is the carob pods. When he tried to take something from them, the owner of the swine rebuked him, so he worked much and ate little, and became exposed to dying of hunger. So the prodigal son was occupied with the pleasures of the world, and at the end he discovered his hunger for righteousness; and instead of returning to his father (God), he again sought in the world for work in order to eat and be satisfied with these material things, and he found an employer, who is Satan, the prince of this world, who sent him to the works of the world, which are his fields, to feed swine. Swine were unclean and forbidden among the Jews, and raising them was not permitted because they represent uncleanness, that is, the works of the world connected with unclean desires.

15.8.1.en: And he found nothing in them to satisfy him, so his hunger increased until he needed to eat the food of the animals, which is the husks. The husks are hollow pods up to 30 cm long that hang from trees and are given to animals.

15.8.2.en: "No man gave unto him": that is, he needed evil and the hollow food that does not satisfy, that is, material things, and did not find it, and he nearly died of hunger and departed from life.

15.8.3.en: Satan lures you with the pleasure of desires until he humiliates you and leads you to destruction. So return quickly through repentance before Satan humiliates you.

15.9.0.en: Here the greatness of repentance appears, and the secret of the strength of this prodigal son, who is also called the clever one, for he came to himself and discovered the results of his sin, which are humiliation and nearness to destruction, and compared himself with his glory in his father's house, and that the lowest person with his father, the hired servant and not the son of the house, has enough to eat and to spare. So he grieved in his heart for his former joy, standing and way of life.

15.9.1.en: He signifies the person who keeps away from the Church in the desires of the world and its various preoccupations, so he loses his joy and is deprived of his spiritual food; and when he is humbled by sin, God reminds him of his first life in the Church, and how the beginner in the spiritual life, whom the hired servant signifies, is spiritually satisfied, and indeed has many opportunities for spiritual food before him. So he longs for repentance and for returning to his sonship to God in the Church.

15.9.2.en: So he decided to return to his father and declare his repentance, that he had sinned against heaven and not only against his father, and with contrition he declares his unworthiness to return in the rank of sonship, but wishes that his father would receive him as a hired servant, that is, the lowest person in the Church.

15.10.0.en: The love of the Father who awaits his son appears; when the son rose and began to move on the way of return, that is, repentance, he found his father running toward him in haste to embrace him and hold him close, not caring about the filthiness of his clothes and body, because God's love forgives all our sins and we become whiter than snow.

15.10.1.en: "And fell on his neck": he lifted from him the yoke of the slavery of sin and also showed his love and tenderness by this fatherly kiss. And when the son began to declare his confession, the father did not let him finish by allowing him to be a hired servant, but stopped him at his declaration of unworthiness of sonship, in order to give him, by his fatherhood, a complete sonship.

15.10.2.en: The tenderness of God is beyond all imagining, and He does not shrink from our sins but by His love lifts them from us and cleanses us from all our iniquities.

15.11.0.en: God showed His fatherhood to His prodigal son by commanding His servants, that is, the priests in the Church, to put on him the best robe, which is the garment of righteousness that we receive in Baptism when our nature is renewed in it (Gal 3:27), or that we receive in the sacrament of repentance and confession; then the ring, which is the seal of the Holy Spirit in the sacrament of the Holy Myron, so that the Holy Spirit may dwell in us permanently (2 Cor 1:21, 22); as for his feet, He gave him shoes, which is walking by the word of God, which confirms sonship (Eph 6:15). The son wears shoes, but the hired laborer has none.

15.11.1.en: As for the fatted calf, it is the Lamb without blemish, Christ our God, who was slain on the cross for our redemption, and we eat Him as true Body and Blood on the altar every day and live by Him (Jn 6:56). And the father declared to all the members of his household that they should rejoice at the return of his prodigal son, who returned to life by his repentance and return to the Church through the Holy Sacraments.

15.12.0.en: The elder son represents the Jews, or the proud, or those connected with God in appearance.

15.12.1.en: The field signifies the world, with which many are occupied.

15.12.3.en: "Musick and dancing": that is, the loud hymns of praise in the Church, in joy at the sinner's return and in thanksgiving to God.

15.13.0.en: "He asked": that is, he read the Holy Bible.

15.13.1.en: "One of the servants": that is, one of the prophets of the Old Testament who prophesied the acceptance of the Gentiles in the salvation of Christ the Redeemer when they returned to Him in repentance and faith.

15.14.0.en: The servant told the elder son of his prodigal brother's return and his father's joy over him because he had come back to the house. He signifies the prophets who wrote of the repentance of sinners and the acceptance of the Gentiles, or he signifies the priests and servants of the New Testament who declare the acceptance of repentant sinners in the Church and their partaking of the Holy Sacraments.

15.15.0.en: The Jews, or the proud in the Church, were distressed and angry at the acceptance of the Gentiles and sinners, and refused to enter the house of God because of their pride.

15.15.1.en: "His father came out": the father's tenderness made him come out to them, seeking the salvation of the Pharisees and the proud Jews also.

15.16.0.en: "Do I serve thee" these many years, with pride: the Pharisees suppose that they have a claim on God by their service to Him.

15.16.1.en: "Neither transgressed I at any time thy commandment": the Pharisees feel their self-righteousness and their complete application of the Law and commandments. The kid signifies the material desires of the world.

15.16.2.en: Pride made them ask for earthly goods and not spiritual food, while the repentant, humble prodigal son was united with Christ in the sacrament of the Eucharist.

15.17.0.en: "This thy son": the proud dared to say to God of their brother "this thy son," disowning him.

15.17.1.en: "Hath devoured thy living": he wasted the gifts that were given to him, for they provoke God against their brothers the sinners. "With harlots": he accused his brother of consorting with harlots, although the parable did not mention this, but only that he wasted his substance; pride made him accuse his brother falsely.

15.17.2.en: Humble yourself so that your eyes may be enlightened and you rejoice at the sinner's acceptance and do not condemn him, and discover God's mercies, of which you are the most needy person.

15.18.0.en: "Son": He showed His fatherhood to him despite his murmuring and his hatred of his brother, for God seeks the salvation of all, including the proud.

15.18.1.en: "All that I have is thine": true sonship has all the divine blessings, and this means that the elder son does not feel his sonship to God.

15.18.2.en: God declared a truth to the Jews and to all those connected with the Church, which is that He has given them His abundant goods and His sure promises, and they ought to have enjoyed them, so as not to fall into pride but to have their hearts opened to love for their brothers the sinners, and even to seek to bring them back and rejoice at their return. For as much as we grieve at a person's death in the body, we rejoice at anyone's rising from death, in the case of his repentance and return if he was a sinner, or his faith if he was not a believer. The parables of the unjust steward and of the rich man and Lazarus. The parable of the unjust steward (vv. 1-8):

15.18.3.en: 1- And he said also unto his disciples, "There was a certain rich man, which had a steward; and the same was accused unto him that he had wasted his goods. 2- And he called him, and said unto him, How is it that I hear this of thee? give an account of thy stewardship; for thou mayest be no longer steward."

15.18.4.en: 3- Then the steward said within himself, What shall I do? for my lord taketh away from me the stewardship: I cannot dig; to beg I am ashamed. 4- I am resolved what to do, that, when I am put out of the stewardship, they may receive me into their houses.

15.18.5.en: 5- So he called every one of his lord's debtors unto him, and said unto the first, How much owest thou unto my lord? 6- And he said, An hundred measures of oil.

15.18.6.en: And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and sit down quickly, and write fifty. 7- Then said he to another, And how much owest thou? And he said, An hundred measures of wheat. And he said unto him, Take thy bill, and write fourscore. 8- And the lord commended the unjust steward, because he had done wisely: for the children of this world are in their generation wiser than the children of light.
